Stated Claim / Post Context:
A 124-year-old voting ban designed to silence Black Virginians is finally gone

Voters passed the amendment by more than 10 points, ending lifetime disenfranchisement for people with felony convictions.

Actual Article Body:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger stands for a portrait outside her ceremonial office at the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond, Va. on Oct. 9, 2026.Francis Chung/Politico/AP

While Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, governors’ mansions, and state legislatures across the country, Virginia overturned its “Jim Crow-era lifetime ban” on voting for people with prior felony convictions.

Voters approved a ballot amendment that restores voting rights to people with felony convictions immediately upon their release, along with two other ballot initiatives that enshrined reproductive rights and same-sex marriage protections in the state’s constitution. The law restoring voting rights to formerly incarcerated people passed by over 10 percentage points with 96.8 percent of votes counted, according to NBC News.

Enacted back in 1902, Virginia’s law banned anyone convicted of a felony from voting for the rest of their lives. Back then, one hundred male white delegates passed this provision with the explicit intent of disenfranchising Black voters. While plenty of other states bar former felons from voting, Virginia was only one of three states, along with Iowa and Kentucky, with this Jim Crow-era law on the books. In February 2026, The Sentencing Project reported that over a quarter of a million Virginians were blocked from voting because of it.

In Tennessee, it’s a felony if you’re found on public property while unhoused. In Kentucky, the state decriminalized the use of deadly force to remove an unhoused person from private property.

I reported earlier this week about the challenges unhoused voters in Virginia face in casting their ballots. In it, I spoke with Donald Whitehead, executive director of the National Coalition for the Homeless, who told me that there’s a revolving door between incarceration and homelessness.
